bubble.e: Partly imitative, also influenced by burble. The word was first used in its economic sense in association with the collapse of the South Sea Company in 1720, based on the metaphor of an inflated soap bubble bursting.
bubble.g: A spherically contained volume of air or other gas in a liquid, commonly a soapy liquid.

bucket.e: From Middle English buket, boket, partly from Old English bucc ("bucket, pitcher"; mod. dialectal buck), equivalent to bouk + -et; and partly from Anglo-Norman buket, buquet (“tub; pail”) (compare Norman boutchet, Norman bouquet), diminutive of Old French buc (“abdomen; object with a cavity”).
bucket.g: A container made of rigid material, often with a handle, used to carry liquids or small items.

buckle.e: Noun etymology 1, noun sense 2 (“great conflict or struggle”) is probably derived from verb etymology 1, verb sense 1.2.1 (“to apply (oneself) to, or prepare (oneself) for, a task or work”).
buckle.g: A metal clasp with a hinged tongue or a spike through which a belt or strap is passed and penetrated by the tongue or spike, in order to fas

buckle.e: Origin uncertain. Probably from Middle English bukklen, bokelen (“to arch the body”), from Middle French boucler (“to bulge”, literally “to take the shape of a shield boss”), perhaps from the same ultimate origin as Etymology 1 above, or perhaps related to Middle Low German bockelen (“to bang out curves in metal”), German buckeln (“to bend over, hunch”).
buckle.g: To cause (something) to bend, or to become distorted.

buckler.e: From Middle English bukler, bokler, bokeler, bokeleer, from Old French bocler, boucler, bucler, (French bouclier) from Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”). Merged with buckle + -er.

buckling.e: From the verb to buckle, equivalent to buckle + -ing.
buckling.g: The act of fastening a buckle.

bud.e: From Middle English budde, bodde (“bud, seed pod”), from Old English *budde, from Proto-West Germanic *buʀdā, from Proto-Germanic *buzdǭ (compare archaic German Butte (“rosehip”), Swedish dialect bodd (“head”)), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bu- (“to swell”). Haagbudden (“rosehips”, plural)).
bud.g: A newly sprouted leaf or blossom that has not yet unfolded.

budge.e: Borrowed from Middle French bouger, from Old French bougier, from Vulgar Latin *bullicāre (“to bubble; seethe; move; stir”), from Latin bullīre (“to boil; seethe; roil”).
budge.g: To move; to be shifted from a fixed position.

budge.e: From Middle English bouge, bougie, bugee, from Anglo-Norman bogé, from Anglo-Latin *bogea, bulgia, related to Latin bulga (“a leathern bag or knapsack”).
budge.g: A kind of fur prepared from lambskin dressed with the wool on, formerly used as an edging and ornament, especially on scholastic habits.

buffet.e: From Middle English buffet (“stool”), from Middle French buffet (“side table”), from Old French buffet, of unknown origin. The modern pronunciation is remodelled after modern French buffet.
buffet.g: A counter or sideboard from which food and drinks are served or may be bought.

buffet.e: From Middle English buffet (“buffet”), from Old French buffet, diminutive of buffe, cognate with Italian buffetto.
buffet.g: A blow or cuff with or as if with the hand, or by any other solid object or the wind.

build.e: From Middle English bilden, buylden, bylden, from Old English byldan and bytlan, bytlian (“to build”), from Proto-West Germanic *buþlijan (“to build”), from Proto-Germanic *buþlą, *bōþlą (“house, dwelling, farm”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”). False cognate of German bilden.
build.g: To form (something) by combining materials or parts.

builder.e: From Middle English bildere, byldere, from bilden + -ere. By surface analysis, build + -er.
builder.g: One who builds or constructs things.

building.e: From Middle English beeldynge, equivalent to build + -ing.

bulge.e: From Middle English bulge (“leather bag; hump”), from Old Northern French boulge (“leather bag”), from Late Latin bulga (“leather sack”), from Gaulish *bulga, *bulgos, from Proto-Celtic *bolgos (“sack, bag, stomach”).
bulge.g: An object which is sticking out from a surface; a swelling, protuberant part; a bending outward, especially when caused by pressure.

bull.e: From Middle English bole, bul, bule, from a conflation of Old English bula (“bull, steer”) and Old Norse boli, both from Proto-Germanic *bulô (“bull”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥no-, from *bʰel- (“to blow, swell up”). Of noun sense 2.6, (a man or boy), derived from the Philadelphia English pronunciation of boy, which is practically a homophone of bull.
From Middle English bowle, boule, from Old French bulle, boule (“ball”), from Latin bulla (“round swelling”), of Gaulish origin.

bullock.e: From Middle English bullok, from Old English bulluc, from Proto-West Germanic *bulluk, corresponding to bull + -ock (diminutive suffix).

bulrush.e: From Middle English bulrish, perhaps from bule (“bull”) (in the sense of "large") + rish (“rush”).
bulrush.g: A plant referred to in the story of Moses as growing along the banks of the Nile, which is believed to be the papyrus (Cyperus papyrus).

bulwark.e: From Middle English bulwerk, from Middle Dutch bolwerk, bolwerc and Middle Low German bolwerk, equivalent to bole (“tree trunk”) + work.

bunch.e: From Middle English bunche, bonche (“hump, swelling”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps a variant of *bunge (compare dialectal bung (“heap, grape bunch”)), from Proto-Germanic *bunkō, *bunkô, *bungǭ (“heap, crowd”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰenǵʰ-, *bʰénǵʰus (“thick, dense, fat”).
bunch.g: A group of similar things, either growing together, or in a cluster or clump, usually fastened together.

bundle.e: From Middle English bundel, from Middle Dutch bondel or Old English byndele, byndelle (“a binding; tying; fastening with bands”); both from Proto-Germanic *bundil-, derivative of *bundą (“bundle”).
bundle.g: A group of objects held together by wrapping or tying.

burden.e: From Middle English birthene, birthen, birden, from Old English byrden, byrþen, from Proto-West Germanic *burþini, from *burþī, from Proto-Germanic *burþį̄, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry, bear”).
From Middle English burdoun (“accompaniment”), from Old French bordon (“drone”), from Medieval Latin burdō.
burden.g: A phrase or theme that recurs at the end of each verse in a folk song or ballad.

burdensome.g: Characteristic of a burden; arduous or demanding.

burial.e: From Middle English biriel, a backformation from biriels, which was re-interpreted as a plural, itself from from Old English byrġels, from byrġan (“to bury”) + -els. By surface analysis, bury + -al, but originally unrelated to this suffix.
burial.g: The act of burying; interment; placing remains into the earth.

burier.e: From bury + -er, from Middle English biriere, from Old English byrgere. Present form probably reformed from the verb based on West Midland dialect.

burn.e: From late Middle English burne, birne, metathetic form of brinne, brynne, a variant of brennen, from Old Norse brinna, brenna (“to burn”), from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną (“to burn”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenw-, present stem from *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil”).
burn.g: A physical injury caused by heat, cold, electricity, radiation or caustic chemicals.

burn.e: From Northern Middle English burn, from Old English burne, burna (“spring, fountain”), Proto-West Germanic *brunnō, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô, *brunō.

burned.e: The past tense is inherited from Middle English burnede. The past participle (from which the adjective is also derived) is inherited from Middle English burned. Synchronically, both forms are equivalent to burn + -ed.
burned.g: Damaged or consumed by heat, fire, oxidation, or similar process.

burning.g: So hot as to seem to burn (something).

burnish.g: To make (something, such as a surface) bright, shiny, and smooth by, or (by extension) as if by, rubbing; to polish, to shine.

burnish.e: From Middle English barnishen, barnish (“to grow big (with child), to become pregnant; to grow stout or strong”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from barn (“child, offspring; infant; unborn child; human being, person; male person, man (especially a young man or young warrior)”). (from Old English bearn (“child”).
burnish.g: Of a person's body: to grow large or stout; to fatten, to fill out.

burnt.e: From Middle English brent, brynt; by surface analysis, burn + t.
burnt.g: Damaged or injured by fire or heat.

burst.e: From Middle English bresten, bersten, from Old English berstan, from Proto-West Germanic *brestan, from Proto-Germanic *brestaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to burst, break, crack, split, separate”), enlargement of *bʰreHi- (“to snip, split”).

bury.e: Middle English birien, berien, from Old English byrġan, from Proto-West Germanic *burgijan, from Proto-Germanic *burgijaną (“to keep safe”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to defend, protect”). West Frisian bergje (“to keep”), German bergen (“to save/rescue something”), Danish bjerge (“to save/rescue something or somebody”).
bury.g: To ritualistically inter in a grave or tomb.

burying.e: From Middle English biryinge, buryinge; by surface analysis, bury + ing.

buryingplace.g: The place where a dead person is buried.

bush.e: From Middle English bush, from Old English *busċ, *bysċ (“copse, grove, scrub”, in placenames), from Proto-West Germanic *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, thicket”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”).
bush.g: A woody plant distinguished from a tree by its multiple stems and lower height, being usually less than six metres tall; a horticultural rat

bush.e: From the sign of a bush usually employed to indicate such places.

bushel.e: From Middle English busshel, from Old French boissel, from boisse, a grain measure based on Gaulish *bostyā (“handful”), from Proto-Celtic *bostā (“palm, fist”) (compare Breton boz (“hollow of the hand”), Old Irish bas), from Proto-Indo-European *gwost-, *gwosdʰ- (“branch”).
bushel.g: A dry measure, containing four pecks, eight gallons, or thirty-two quarts; equivalent in volume to approximately 0.0364 cubic meters (imperi

business.e: From Middle English busines, busynes, businesse, bisynes, from Old English bisiġnes (“business, busyness”), equivalent to busy + -ness. Sense 17 (something very good, top quality), possibly derives from "the bee's knees"
business.g: A specific commercial enterprise or establishment.

bustle.e: From Middle English bustlen, bustelen, bostlen, perhaps an alteration of *busklen (> Modern English buskle), a frequentative of Middle English busken (“to prepare; make ready”), from Old Norse búask (“to prepare oneself”); or alternatively from a frequentative form of Middle English busten, bisten (“to buffet; pummel; dash; beat”) + -le.

busy.e: From Middle English bisy, busie, from Old English bisiġ (“busy, occupied, diligent”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisīg (“diligent; zealous; busy”). The spelling with ⟨u⟩ represents the pronunciation of the West Midland and Southern dialects while the Modern English pronunciation with /ɪ/ is from the dialects of the East Midlands.
busy.g: Crowded with business or activities; having a great deal going on.

busy.e: From Middle English bisien, from Old English bisgian (“to occupy, employ, trouble, afflict”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisīgōn.
busy.g: To make somebody busy or active; to occupy.

but.e: From Middle English but, buten, boute, bouten, from Old English būtan (“without, outside of, except, only”), from Proto-West Germanic *biūtan, *biūtini, equivalent to be- + out.

butcher.e: From Middle English bocher, boucher, from Old French bouchier (“goat slaughterer”), from Old French bouc (“goat”), from Medieval Latin buccus (“he-goat”), from Frankish *bukk, from Proto-Germanic *bukkaz (“male goat, male deer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuǵ- (“buck, ram”).
butcher.g: A person who prepares and sells meat (and sometimes also slaughters the animals).

butler.e: From Middle English butler, butlere, boteler, botelere, from Old French buttiler, butiller, boteillier (“officer in charge of wine”), from Medieval Latin botellārius, equivalent to bottle + -er. Piecewise doublet of bottler.
butler.g: A manservant having charge of wines and liquors.

butlership.e: From Middle English buttlershipe, equivalent to butler + -ship.
butlership.g: The rank, office, or position of a butler.

butt.e: From Middle English but, butte (“goal, mark, butt of land”), from Old English byt, bytt (“small piece of land”) and *butt (attested in diminutive Old English buttuc (“end, small piece of land”) > English buttock), from Proto-West Germanic *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz (“end, piece”).
butt.g: The larger or thicker end of something; the blunt end, in distinction from the sharp or narrow end.

butt.e: From Middle English butten, from Anglo-Norman buter, boter (“to push, butt, strike”), from Frankish *bautan (“to hit, beat”), from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to beat, push”).
butt.g: To strike bluntly, particularly with the head.

butter.e: From Middle English buter, butter, from Old English butere, from Proto-West Germanic *buterā, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron, “cow cheese”), compound of βοῦς (boûs, “ox, cow”) and τῡρός (tūrós, “cheese”).
butter.g: A soft, fatty foodstuff made by churning the cream of milk (generally cow's milk).

buttock.e: From Middle English buttok, probably from Old English buttuc (“end; end piece”; also, “short piece of land”). A diminutive form of what is presumably the Old English precursor of butt + -ock (diminutive suffix).
buttock.g: Each of the two large fleshy halves of the posterior part of the body between the base of the back, the perineum, and the top of the legs.

buy.e: From Middle English byen, from Old English bycġan (“to buy, pay for, acquire, redeem, ransom, procure, get done, sell”), from Proto-West Germanic *buggjan, from Proto-Germanic *bugjaną (“to buy”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰūgʰ- (“to bend”), or from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to take away, deliver”).
buy.g: To obtain (something) in exchange for money or goods.
